intro: The Osteosarcoma — Toronto Stage is a oncology scoring tool used in paediatric practice. Staged by the presence of metastases at diagnosis. It scores 1 criteria and interprets the total across 2 bands, so the number always arrives with the severity it implies rather than on its own. In PediAid each criterion is shown as a labelled option with the weight it carries, so the total can be checked rather than taken on trust.
indications: Grading severity at the bedside in oncology
Recording an objective severity band in the case notes
Deciding when a total crosses the threshold for escalation
Re-scoring to track whether a child is improving or deteriorating
Checking the exact criteria of a score used infrequently
method: The score sums 1 criteria: Disease extent at diagnosis. Totals are then banded: 1 stage or more - Stage I - localised: localised osteosarcoma - approximately 60-70% long-term survival with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, limb-salvage surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy; 2 stage or more - Stage II - metastatic: metastatic osteosarcoma - approximately 20-30% survival. Aggressive chemotherapy plus resection of all resectable metastases.
guidelineRefs: Histological necrosis ≥90% after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is a favourable prognostic factor.
Source: Gupta S, Aitken JF, Bartels U et al. Paediatric cancer stage in population-based cancer registries: the Toronto consensus principles and guidelines. Lancet Oncol 2016;17:e163-72.

faqs.q: How many criteria does the Osteosarcoma — Toronto Stage use?
faqs.a: 1. They are Disease extent at diagnosis.

faqs.q: What do the bands of the Osteosarcoma — Toronto Stage mean?
faqs.a: The total is interpreted as: 1 stage or more - Stage I - localised: localised osteosarcoma - approximately 60-70% long-term survival with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, limb-salvage surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy; 2 stage or more - Stage II - metastatic: metastatic osteosarcoma - approximately 20-30% survival. Aggressive chemotherapy plus resection of all resectable metastases.

faqs.q: Does the score replace clinical judgement?
faqs.a: No. It is a structured way to record and communicate severity. A clinician concerned about a child should act on that concern regardless of the total.
